analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share parts, tools, and manuals so owners and independent shops can fix devices.
analysis.headline: The Fair Repair Act was introduced in the Senate in May 2024, referred to the Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require makers of digital electronics — phones, laptops, appliances, and similar products — to sell or provide documentation, parts, and repair tools to independent repair shops and device owners on the same terms they give their own authorized repair network. It would also ban "parts pairing," a practice where software blocks a device from fully working with a replacement part the manufacturer did not approve. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules. The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who own or lease electronics, and the independent repair shops that serve them. Owners would be able to get manuals, schematics, parts, and diagnostic tools at the same price and terms the manufacturer offers its own repair network, and could use third-party or used parts without the device being deliberately degraded or hit with false warning messages. Independent shops would compete on even terms with manufacturer-authorized repair.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools — including updates — available to owners and independent repair providers on terms equivalent to the most favorable terms offered to their own authorized repair providers.

The bill bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that block functional replacement parts, reduce device performance after independent repair, trigger false or non-dismissible warnings, add fees for future repairs, or limit who can buy parts.
The FTC would enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue to stop violations and obtain penalties, damages, and restitution for residents.
For devices with security locks, manufacturers would have to provide what is needed to disable and reset the lock during repair, so security features could not be used to lock out independent repair.

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers of digital electronics — phone, computer, appliance, and similar device makers — which would lose control over who repairs their products and the pricing power that comes with being the only authorized source of parts and service.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and some security researchers have long argued that broad access to repair documentation, security codes, and lock-disabling tools can create security and safety risks, and the bill would require manufacturers to hand over tools to disable electronic security locks on devices.
The bill does not apply to motor vehicles or medical devices, two large categories where repair restrictions are common, so farmers, car owners, and hospitals would get no new rights under this bill.
Manufacturers could still withhold information they classify as a trade secret except as needed to provide documentation, parts, and tools, leaving room to contest what must be disclosed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for consumers are concrete: cheaper repairs, more repair options, longer-lasting devices, and less electronic waste. The main counterweights are the security and safety concerns manufacturers raise about disclosing lock-disabling tools, and the fact that the bill's scope stops short of cars and medical devices, which limits how much it would change day-to-day repair access. On balance the bill is a straightforward consumer-and-small-business measure whose main cost falls on manufacturers' repair revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the Fair Repair Act in the Senate on May 23, 2024, joined by Senator Ron Wyden.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Senate Democrat, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics manufacturers keep the status quo: they remain the gatekeepers of parts, tools, and repair information and continue to control the repair market and its prices. Consumers and independent repair shops remain in the position they were in, paying whatever the manufacturers' authorized system charges.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll-call picture exists; its two co-introducers and sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican support was recorded.

industries.note: These companies make money by controlling who can repair their devices — restricting parts, pairing components to block third-party parts, and channeling repairs through authorized providers at OEM-set prices. The bill would end those restrictions, cutting into their repair and parts revenue while saving consumers money.
Shops would get the same manuals, parts, tools, and pricing that authorized providers get, letting them compete for repair work they are currently locked out of or pay premiums to perform.

Authorized providers would keep their warranty and recall arrangements, but they would lose the near-exclusive access to parts and tools that currently gives them an advantage over independent competitors.
